'''''Magnolia tripetala''''', commonly called '''umbrella magnolia''' or simply '''umbrella-tree''',  is a [[deciduous]] [[tree]] native to the eastern [[United States]] in the [[Appalachian Mountains]], the [[Ozarks]], and the [[Ouachita Mountains]].  The name "umbrella tree" derives from the fact that the large leaves are clustered at the tips of the branches forming an [[umbrella]]-shaped structure.

==Description==
Umbrella magnolias have large shiny [[leaf|leaves]] 30–50 cm long, spreading from stout [[Plant stem|stems]]. In a [[nature|natural]] setting the umbrella magnolia can grow 15 m tall. The [[flower]]s are large, appear in the spring, malodorous,<ref name=ef /> 15–25 cm diameter, with six to nine creamy-white [[tepals]] and a large red style, which later develops into a red [[fruit]] (an [[aril]]) 10 cm long, containing several red [[seed]]s. These trees are attractive and easy to grow. The leaves turn [[yellow]] in the autumn. The leaves are clustered at the tip of the stem with very short internodes. The tree has reddish cone-shaped fruit, is shade tolerant, has shallow spreading roots, and is pollinated by beetles.

Leaves on ''M. tripetala'' trees are alternate, simple, and oblong. They are a dark green on top and pale green underneath the leaves. These leaves are clustered at the ends of branches, giving them the appearance of an umbrella. The leaves and arrangement resemble their relative ''[[Magnolia macrophylla|M. macrophylla]]''.<ref name=bernheim>{{Cite web |title=umbrella magnolia |url=https://bernheim.org/learn/trees-plants/bernheim-select-urban-trees/umbrella-magnolia/ |access-date=2023-12-05 |website=Bernheim Arboretum and Research Forest |date=18 July 2023 }}</ref> These trees are naturally in rich and moist woods, along slopes, streams and ravines. The bark is thin and gray, mostly smooth and can have raised lenticels.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Umbrella Magnolia (Magnolia tripetala) |url=http://fwf.ag.utk.edu/dendro/species/umbmgnl.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=fwf.ag.utk.edu}}</ref> Trees typically grow from single stems, though multiple stems are not uncommon.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Magnolia Tripetala (Umbrella Magnolia) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/magnolia-tripetala |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=Gardenia}}</ref> The flowers on ''M. tripetala'' have been described to have unpleasant smells but are not toxic to organisms. These trees grow at a moderate rate during the spring season.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=''Magnolia tripetala'' (L.) L. |website=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=MATR |access-date=2023-11-11}}</ref> 

== Taxonomy ==
The name ''M. tripetala'' was originally described by Linnaeus in his ''[[Systema Naturae]]'' in 1759.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Magnolia tripetala {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://ipni.org/n/554866-1 |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=ipni.org}}</ref> It is most commonly known as the umbrella magnolia or the umbrella tree.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linnaeus |title=Systema Naturae |year=1759 |edition=10th}}</ref> Tripetala comes from Latin and means "three petals". This naming convention was used for the three petal-like sepals of the tree's flowers.<ref name=bernheim/> ''Magnolia tripetala'' is the accepted name of the species but has gone through multiple authors naming the species differently.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Magnolia tripetala (L.) L. |website=WFO Plant List |url=https://wfoplantlist.org/plant-list/taxon/wfo-0000233440-2023-06?page=1 |access-date=2023-11-11}}</ref> Synonyms for ''M. tripetala'' include ''Kobus tripetala, Magnolia frondosa, Magnolia umbrella, Magnolia virginiana var. tripetala,'' and ''Magnolia umbrella var. tripetala''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Magnolia tripetala |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Magnolia_tripetala |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref> 

== Distribution and habitat ==
Umbrella magnolias have a native range from New York state to southern Florida. This range also expands as far west as Arkansas and parts of Oklahoma.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=''Magnolia tripetala'' Umbrella Magnolia |work=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.147677/Magnolia_tripetala |access-date=2023-10-18}}</ref> It is located in deciduous forests of the Appalachian Mountains.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Rhoads |first=Ann F. |date=1994 |title=Magnolia tripetala in Pennsylvania |jstor=41610024 |journal=Bartonia |volume=58 |issue=58 |pages=75–77}}</ref> Research has shown the species to be non-native to northern states such as Pennsylvania, and only being a recent arrival.<ref name=":2"/> This species has been cultivated in locations outsides its natural range, and has spread from these locations to nearby woodlands.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |title=Magnolia Tripetala |work=Pennsylvania Natural Heritage Program}}</ref> ''Magnolia tripetala'' has been observed in forests outside its native range in multiple instances. Single individuals and small populations have been observed near areas where ''M. tripetala'' is in cultivation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bellemare |first=Jesse |date=1 July 2015 |title=Horticultural Escape and Naturalization of Magnolia tripetala in Western Massachusetts: Biogeographic Context and Possible Relationship to Recent Climate Change |url=https://meridian.allenpress.com/rhodora/article-abstract/117/971/371/110062/Horticultural-Escape-and-Naturalization-of |journal=Rhodora: Journal of the New England Botanical Club |volume=117 |issue=971 |pages=371–383}}</ref> ''Magnolia tripetala'' has been given the FACU wetland status, tending to prefer average to dry soil.<ref name=":1"/> The trees have low tolerance to drought and fire.
==Reproduction== 
''Magnolia tripetala'' in cultivation can produce low viability pollen (9.4-31.7%). Actual seed productivity of the ''M. tripetala'' is less than their potential productivity. However, ''M. tripetala'' are characterized by a high seed germination rates, up to 94%. Optimal seed germination conditions for ''M. tripetala'' are protected ground or a greenhouse and stratification at 4 °C for 30 days.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kameneva |first1=L. A. |last2=Koksheeva |first2=I. M. |date=2013 |title=Reproductive biology of seven taxa of Magnolia L. in the south of Russian Far East |journal=Bangladesh Journal of Plant Taxonomy |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=163–170 |doi=10.3329/bjpt.v20i2.17390|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Notable trees==
The largest known ''Magnolia tripetala'' is 15.2 m in height with a trunk diameter of 87 cm in [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="ef">{{cite web|title=Magnolia tripetala|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=233500771|website=Flora of North America|access-date=8 November 2015}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Magnolia tripetala'' contains a substance called [[ethyl acetate]] in its branches, and this substance displays nematicidal activity.<ref name=NtalliCaboni>{{cite journal |last1=Ntalli |first1=N. G. |last2=Caboni |first2=P. |date=2012 |title=Botanical nematicides: a review |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |volume=60 |issue=40 |pages=9929–9940|doi=10.1021/jf303107j |pmid=22973877 }}</ref> This activity allows it to specifically resist ''[[Bursaphelenchus xylophilus]]'', ''[[Panagrellus redivivus]]'', and ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans]]''.<ref name=NtalliCaboni/>

''Magnolia tripetala'' has been used as a parent with ''[[Magnolia obovata]]'' (Japanese cucumber tree), resulting in the hybrid ''Magnolia x pruhoniciana'', an ornamental plant. This hybrid is named for the park for which it was first discovered, Prühonice Park in the Czech Republic.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=''Magnolia'' × ''pruhoniciana'' |website=Trees and Shrubs Online |url=https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/magnolia/magnolia-x-pruhoniciana/#19682 |access-date=2023-11-11}}</ref> The hybrid has resulted in multiple hybrid variants, including the named 'Silk Road' and 'Silver Parasol' cultivars. The variants are described to be deciduous, medium trees with elliptic to ovate leaves. The leaves are 20-45cm by 10-22cm and the flowers are white, 16-25cm across at the end of branches. The cultivars have fruits with features such as number of follicles or stamen scars that are intermediate between the parent species.<ref name=":5"/>

Umbrella magnolia leaves are eaten by a variety of animals. They often grow under the canopy of larger trees and support biodiversity in forested areas.<ref name=":1"/> These trees are notably used as specimen trees for their unique foliage. ''Magnolia tripetala'' is used as an ornamental in urban areas and used as focal trees in the garden setting.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=''Magnolia tripetala'' |website=Florida Native Plant Society (FNPS) |url=https://www.fnps.org/plant/magnolia-tripetala |access-date=2023-11-11}}</ref>

== Diseases ==
Umbrella magnolias are victim to pests such as magnolia scales or [[Yellow-Poplar Weevil|yellow poplar weevils]]. Magnolia scales infest and slowly kill branches of many trees, including species of magnolias. Yellow poplar weevils infest the leaves of magnolias and can cause mortality.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Magnolia tripetala (Umbrella Magnolia, Umbrella-tree) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/magnolia-tripetala/ |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
''Magnolia tripetala'' has a secure conservation status across multiple states in most of its native range. However there are multiple states where the tree is considered critically imperiled or exotic. Many states within the native range of ''M. tripetala'' have not assessed its endangerment status. States where there is no status ranking (SNR/SU/SNA) for ''M. tripetala'' include Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. States where the tree is considered secure (S5) include North Carolina, Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky. ''Magnolia tripetala'' is critically imperiled (S1) in Oklahoma, Mississippi, Florida, and Indiana. Global status for ''M. tripetala'' is secure (G5) as of 1991. Global status is in need of review.<ref name=":2"/> Efforts to conserve ''M. tripetala'' have been taken by local and state-wide ecological groups and are still being recommended. As the tree grows on steep slopes, the trees and soil are subject to damage due to human traffic in its native range. ''Ailanthus altissima'' has been described as a competitor to ''M. tripetala'' and has been removed from its habitat to better support ''M. tripetala'' persistence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Badger |last2=Jackson |first1=Kemuel |first2=Marion T. |date=1983 |title=A Study of the Natural History of Naturally Occurring Populations of Magnolia tripetala L. in Indiana |journal=Proceedings of the Indiana Academy of Science |volume=93 |pages=309–312 |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?view_op=view_citation&hl=en&user=rocd9loAAAAJ&sortby=title&citation_for_view=rocd9loAAAAJ:W7OEmFMy1HYC}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
''Magnolia tripetala'' most commonly lives in slope forests on north-facing slopes.<ref name=":6"/> The tree has been seen to grow along streambanks as well as in many ravines.<ref name=":4"/> Beetles are the primary pollinators of ''M. tripetala'' and birds and squirrels disperse seeds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Umbrella magnolia |url=https://mortonarb.org/plant-and-protect/trees-and-plants/umbrella-magnolia/ |access-date=2023-10-18 |website=The Morton Arboretum}}</ref> Beetles enter buds of the flowers to feed on pollen and move this pollen from male parts of the flower to female parts. The male reproductive parts of the flower mature first.<ref name=":6"/> These trees are slow to spread but seedlings are resilient. Flowers bloom in the spring while seeds mature and spread throughout the summer.<ref name=":1"/>
